reason: The sources provide robust, multi-site evidence detailing the discovery, physics, acoustic scale, and sonification of the Perseus black hole sound waves.
story: Space is widely known as a silent vacuum, but galaxy clusters break the rule. At the core of the Perseus Cluster, 250 million light-years away, a supermassive black hole pumps enormous energy into the surrounding multimillion-degree gas. In 2002, NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory captured concentric ripples spreading across hundreds of thousands of light-years in the cluster's X-ray glow. Astronomers discovered these ripples were acoustic pressure waves generated by plasma bubbles blown by the black hole. The acoustic pitch was calculated to be a B-flat, exactly 57 octaves below middle C—the deepest cosmic note ever recorded. Its oscillation period is an astounding 9.6 million years, over a quadrillion times below the limits of human hearing. The tremendous energy carried by this cosmic hum prevents cluster gas from cooling and forming stars. Decades later, NASA sonified the waves by scaling their frequency up 144 quadrillion times, finally allowing humanity to hear the roar of a black hole.
angle: A supermassive black hole 250 million light-years away sings a continuous B-flat pitched 57 octaves below middle C, a sound wave so deep that a single oscillation takes nearly ten million years.

claims.claim: NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory detected acoustic pressure waves radiating from a supermassive black hole in the Perseus Cluster.
The Perseus Cluster lies approximately 250 million light-years away from Earth.
Sound waves can propagate through the Perseus Cluster because it is filled with a vast cloud of hot gas providing a physical medium.
The sound waves are visible in X-ray imaging as concentric ripples traveling through the hot intracluster gas.
The true pitch of the Perseus black hole note is 57 octaves below middle C on a piano.
In musical notation, the pitch translates specifically to the note of B-flat.
The frequency of the Perseus sound wave is over one quadrillion times deeper than the limits of human hearing.
The sound waves are produced by bubbles of relativistic plasma blown into the cluster by the central galaxy NGC 1275.
The Perseus galaxy cluster is the brightest cluster in the sky when observed in the X-ray band.
Generating the cavities that emit the sound waves requires energy equivalent to 100 million supernovae.
The energy dissipated by the sound waves heats the intracluster gas, keeping it warm and preventing it from cooling to form stars.
The study detecting the deepest sound note was led by astronomer Andrew Fabian of Cambridge University.
NASA sonified the Perseus data by scaling the sound waves upward by 57 and 58 octaves to bring them into the range of human hearing.
The sonification sped up the true frequency by 144 quadrillion and 288 quadrillion times.
A similar deep sound phenomenon was identified in the Virgo Cluster around the supermassive black hole in galaxy Messier 87.

disputed: The 9.6 million year wave period is explicitly noted in S1, whereas S5/S6 focus on the 57-octave figure and 2.5 billion year duration without quoting the 9.6 million year period; scripts should state the pitch as 57 octaves below middle C and attribute the multi-million-year period to Cambridge analysis.

The exact discovery year is listed as 2002 for observations in S5 and S6, while formal announcement and papers date to 2003 (S1, S5); scripts can clarify observations were captured in 2002 and announced in 2003.
